title: Marketing environmentally-friendly products

paragraphs.text: Marketing ‘green’ products successfully involves meeting two objectives: providing worthwhile environmental benefits and achieving customer satisfaction. Misjudging either or overemphasizing the former at the expense of the latter can be seen as a mistake. In 1960, Harvard Business Professor Dr Theodore Levitt introduced the concept of short-sighted marketing, terming it ‘marketing myopia’. He characterized a common pitfall of companies as focusing on ‘managing products’ (that is, focusing on the product features, functions and efficient production etc.) instead of ‘meeting customers’ needs’ (that is adapting to consumer expectations and anticipating their future desires). Levitt warned against a corporate preoccupation with products rather than consumer needs. In fact, research indicates that many products have failed because of green marketing myopia – marketers’ short-sighted focus on their products’ ‘greenness’ over the broader expectations of consumers or other market players, such as regulators or activists.

General Motors (GM) and Ford, for example, encountered problems when they launched their EV-1 and Think Mobility electric vehicles in the late 1990s in response to the 1990 zero-emission vehicle regulations which were adopted in California. Both automakers believed their novel two-seater cars would be market successes. GM decided to offer the EV-1 through an attractive lease program, while Ford’s Think Mobility vehicle could be rented via a car-rental chain. Consumers, however, found the electric vehicles’ frequent need to be hooked up to an electrical supply too time-consuming. Critics accused the manufacturers of making only token efforts to market the cars, but a GM spokesman explained, ‘We spent more than $1 billion on producing and promoting the vehicle but fewer than 800 were leased.’ The cars were eventually withdrawn from the market.

Green marketing myopia can also occur when products fail to provide credible, substantive environmental benefits. Mobil’s Hefty plastic trash or rubbish bag is a case in point. Introduced in 1989, Hefty bags prominently displayed the word ‘biodegradable’ with the explanation that a special ingredient in the plastic promoted its decomposition into harmless particles in landfill sites when ‘activated by exposure to the elements’ – sun, wind and rain. However, as most garbage is buried in landfills that allow minimal exposure to the elements, making degradation virtually impossible, the claim enraged environmentalists. Ultimately, attorneys in seven states sued Mobil on charges of broader advertising and consumer fraud. Mobil removed the claim from its packaging and vowed to exercise greater oversight regarding the environmental claims it made.

Some other environmental products, however, have managed to achieve considerable market success. Consider the Toyota Prius, the gasoline-electric hybrid vehicle. Toyota’s production has hardly managed to keep pace with the growing number of customers wishing to purchase the Prius. Consequently, other automakers have rushed to launch their own hybrids. However, despite higher gasoline prices, analysts claim that it can take up to twenty years for the lower running costs to offset the higher price of a hybrid. Several reasons have been suggested for the success of the Prius. Initially, it got a boost at the 2003 Academy Awards when film stars such as Cameron Diaz and Harrison Ford abandoned the usual stretch limousines and arrived in Priuses to mark their support for the campaign to reduce America’s dependence on oil. The Prius was later named Motor Trend’s Car of the Year in 2004. The appeal of the car illustrates that some green products can leverage consumers’ desire to be different. More recently the Prius has gained fans for more practical reasons. A 2006 Maritz poll found that owners purchase hybrids for the convenience of fewer fill-ups, better performance and the enjoyment of driving the latest technology. In some states too, high-mileage hybrid vehicles are allowed to park without payment and are granted solo-occupancy access to high-occupancy vehicle lanes. In conclusion, hybrids offer consumers several desirable benefits that are not necessarily ‘green’.

Past research suggests that in order to be persuasive, green claims should be specific and meaningful. Toyota recognizes the ambiguity of the term ‘green’ and discourages its use in marketing. One proposed slogan, ‘Drive green, breathe blue’ was dismissed in favor of ‘Less gas in. Less gases out.’ Further, environmental claims must be consistent. When Ford publicized its new eco-designed buildings in its Rouge River facility that incorporated the world’s largest ‘living’ roof of plants, critics questioned the authenticity of Ford’s environmental commitment, given the poor fuel economy of the automaker’s best-selling 4-wheel-drive Sports Utility Vehicles (SUVs).

Increasingly, consumers are growing skeptical of commercial messages and are turning to the collective wisdom and experience of their friends and peers. Word-of-mouth or ‘buzz’ is perceived as very credible, especially when consumers are trying to comprehend innovative new products. The internet, through email and its vast, accessible repository of information – websites, search engines, blogs, product rating sites and other digital platforms – has created significant opportunities to spread credible ‘word-of-mouse’ (internet facilitated buzz) about green products. Business has tended to view green marketing as a ‘fringe’ area, given that environmentalism’s acceptance of limits and conservation does not fit with marketing’s traditional assumptions of ‘give customers what they want’ and ‘sell as much as you can’. Sustainability, however, is destined to dominate 21st-century commerce. Rising energy prices, growing pollution and resource consumption, combined with climate change are driving innovation towards healthier, more efficient products. In short, all marketing will have to incorporate elements of green marketing. As the authors of Natural Capitalism argue, a more sustainable business model requires ‘product dematerialization’, that is a shift from the sale of goods to the sale of services (for example, from selling light bulbs to selling illumination). This model is illustrated, if unintentionally, by what is arguably the hottest product of the decade – Apple’s iPod. This allows consumers the convenience of downloading, storing and playing thousands of songs without the environmental impact of manufacturing and distributing CDs, plastic cases and packaging.
